q1: SELECT ITM.ITEMN, ITPV.VENDN FROM ITM ITM, (SELECT DISTINCT ITP.ITEMN, PUR.VENDN FROM ITP ITP, PUR PUR WHERE ITP.PONUM = PUR.PONUM AND PUR.ODATE > 85) ITPV WHERE ITM.ITEMN = ITPV.ITEMN AND ITM.ITEMN > 1 AND ITM.ITEMN < 20
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITM.ITEMN, PUR.VENDN FROM ITM ITM, ITP ITP, PUR PUR WHERE ITP.PONUM = PUR.PONUM AND ITM.ITEMN = ITP.ITEMN AND PUR.ODATE > 85 AND ITM.ITEMN > 1 AND ITM.ITEMN < 20
explanation:
After analysing the two statements we could not find any relational situation that makes them deliver different tuples.

•  Both queries keep exactly the same selection predicates (ODATE > 85, ITEMN between 2 and 19).
•  Both demand the same joins: ITM.ITEMN = ITP.ITEMN and ITP.PONUM = PUR.PONUM.
•  Q1 applies DISTINCT inside the derived table, whereas Q2 applies DISTINCT at the end – but in either case duplicates on the projected columns (ITEMN,VENDN) disappear.  Because ITM has a primary-key on ITEMN there is no other source of duplicates, so the bag difference vanishes.

Consequently the two queries always return the same (set) result on every database that satisfies the given schema constraints.  Hence a counter-example database does not exist.
counterexample_dsp: No database instance can make the results diverge; the queries are equivalent.

q1: SELECT Z.A, Z.B FROM R1 X, R2 Y, R2 Z WHERE X.A = Y.A AND Y.A = Z.A AND X.A = Z.A AND Y.B = Z.B
q2: SELECT Z.A, Z.B FROM R1 X, R2 Y, R2 Z WHERE X.A = Y.A AND Y.A = Z.A AND X.A = Z.A
explanation: Q2 only requires the attribute A to match between the three table instances, while Q1 adds an extra join filter Y.B = Z.B.  Because SQL regards NULL = NULL as UNKNOWN (not TRUE), this extra condition eliminates rows whose B is NULL.  Therefore, whenever the matching R2 row has B IS NULL, Q2 will return it but Q1 will not, so the two queries are not equivalent.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO R1 (A, B) VALUES (1, 100);
INSERT INTO R2 (A, B) VALUES (1, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Give R1 one row with A = 1.  Give R2 one row with the same A = 1 and B = NULL.  The self-join in Q2 succeeds (A matches) and returns (1, NULL).  In Q1 the additional predicate Y.B = Z.B evaluates to UNKNOWN (NULL = NULL), the join is rejected, and the result set is empty.

q1: SELECT ITEMPRICE.NP, ITM.TYPE, ITM.ITEMNO FROM (SELECT DISTINCT ITP.ITEMNO AS ITN, ITP.NP AS NP FROM ITP ITP WHERE ITP.NP > 1000) ITEMPRICE, ITM ITM WHERE ITEMPRICE.ITN = ITM.ITEMNO
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITP.NP, ITM.TYPE, ITM.ITEMNO FROM ITP ITP, ITM ITM WHERE ITP.NP > 1000 AND ITP.ITEMNO = ITM.ITEMNO
explanation: After a careful, step-by-step examination it turns out that Q1 and Q2 are actually equivalent for every possible database that satisfies the given schema constraints.  The only potential source of divergence is the placement of DISTINCT (inside the sub-query in Q1, at the outer level in Q2).  Yet, because ITM.ITEMNO is a primary key and because both queries (1) filter ITP rows with NP > 1000 before the join and (2) ultimately remove duplicate (ITEMNO , NP) combinations, they invariably return exactly the same set of triples (NP , TYPE , ITEMNO).  Therefore no counter-example can be produced.
counterexample_dsp: Not applicable – the two queries always yield identical results.

q1: SELECT ITM.ITEMNO, ITEMPRICE.NP FROM (SELECT DISTINCT ITP.ITEMNO AS ITN, ITP.NP AS NP FROM ITP ITP) ITEMPRICE, ITM ITM WHERE ITEMPRICE.ITN = ITM.ITEMNO
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITM.ITEMNO, ITP.NP FROM ITP ITP, ITM ITM WHERE ITP.ITEMNO = ITM.ITEMNO
explanation: After the DISTINCT has been applied inside Q1’s sub-query, every remaining row is a unique (ITEMNO , NP) pair.  The final join can therefore add at most one copy of that pair (ITM has a primary-key on ITEMNO, so it holds at most one matching row).  Q2 first performs the same join and then applies DISTINCT on the same two columns, removing any duplicates that may have been introduced by repeated rows in ITP.  The final result of both queries is therefore the set of all different (ITEMNO , NP) pairs that appear in ITP for which ITEMNO also exists in ITM – hence the two queries are equivalent for every legal database state.
counterexample_dsp: Because the two queries are logically equivalent, no counter-example (i.e. no data set that makes them return different results) can be constructed without violating the given schema constraints.

q1: SELECT * FROM ITP ITP WHERE ITP.ITEMN IN (SELECT ITL.ITEMN FROM ITL ITL WHERE ITL.WKCEN = 468 AND ITL.LOCAN = 0)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITP.* FROM ITP ITP, ITL ITL WHERE ITP.ITEMN = ITL.ITEMN AND ITL.WKCEN = 468 AND ITL.LOCAN = 0
explanation:
Q1 and Q2 always return exactly the same set of rows.  Both look for those ITEMN-keys that occur in ITL with (WKCEN = 468 AND LOCAN = 0) and then project the corresponding row from ITP.
• Q1 does this with an IN-subquery.
• Q2 does it through an inner join and eliminates any possible duplication with DISTINCT.

Because ITP has a primary-key on ITEMN, each ITEMN can appear only once in ITP, so the DISTINCT in Q2 never removes (or adds) anything.  The two predicates (IN vs. join) are also equivalent when NULL values are present in ITL.ITEMN, and ITP.ITEMN itself is NOT NULL by definition of a PRIMARY KEY.  Therefore no legal database (one that respects the given schema) can make the two result sets diverge.
counterexample_dsp: No counter-example exists under the supplied schema.

q1: SELECT T.TMEMBER FROM DEPTS D, TEAMS T WHERE D.DPROJ = T.TPROJ AND D.DNAME = 'SECURITY'
q2: SELECT V1.E FROM (SELECT D.DNAME AS D, D.DPROJ AS P, P.EMPL AS E FROM DEPTS D, PAYROLL P WHERE D.DNAME = P.PDEPT) V1, (SELECT T.TMEMBER AS E, P.PDEPT AS D, T.TPROJ AS P FROM TEAMS T, PAYROLL P WHERE T.TMEMBER = P.EMPL) V2 WHERE V1.D = 'SECURITY' AND V1.P = V2.P AND V1.E = V2.E AND V1.D = V2.D
explanation: Q1 joins DEPTS with TEAMS on the project-id and only checks that the department name of the DEPTS row is ‘SECURITY’.  Q2, however, first couples every employee with *his/her own* payroll row and additionally demands that the employee’s payroll department (PDEPT) is also ‘SECURITY’ (because V1.D = V2.D = 'SECURITY').  Therefore Q2 filters out employees whose project belongs to the SECURITY department but whose payroll record shows a different department, while Q1 still keeps them.  Hence the two queries are not equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: Create one SECURITY department (project 1).  Put employee 100 on that project in TEAMS, but give the employee a payroll department of 'OTHER'.  Q1 will return 100, Q2 returns nothing.

q1: SELECT Y.* FROM PAYROLL X, APPLICANT Y WHERE X.SSNO = Y.SSNO AND X.DEPTNO = 29
q2: SELECT C.* FROM PAYROLL A, (SELECT Y.SSNO, Y.DEPTNO FROM PAYROLL Y) B, APPLICANT C WHERE A.SSNO = B.SSNO AND C.SSNO = A.SSNO AND B.DEPTNO = 29
schema:
CREATE TABLE PAYROLL (SSNO INT, DEPTNO INT);
CREATE TABLE APPLICANT (SSNO INT, JOBTITILE INT, OFFICENO INT);
explanation: Both queries return applicant rows whose SSNO appears in PAYROLL with DEPTNO = 29.  However, Q1 joins APPLICANT with a single copy of PAYROLL, while Q2 joins APPLICANT with TWO copies of PAYROLL that are only required to share the same SSNO (A.SSNO = B.SSNO).  For every qualifying B-row (DEPTNO = 29) Q2 multiplies the result by the number of PAYROLL rows that have the same SSNO (the A copy).  Therefore Q2 can return the same applicant row more times than Q1 whenever an SSNO has more than one PAYROLL record.  Under SQL’s multiset (bag) semantics the two queries are not equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: SSNO 1 has two PAYROLL records (one in department 29 and one in department 30) and a single APPLICANT record.  Q1 returns the applicant once, Q2 returns it twice.

q1: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP X WHERE (X.EMP, X.DEPT) IN (SELECT Y.MGR, Y.DEPT FROM DEPT Y WHERE Y.LOC = 3)
q2: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP X, DEPT Y WHERE X.DEPT = Y.DEPT AND Y.LOC = 3 AND X.EMP = Y.MGR
schema:
CREATE TABLE EMP (NAME INT, DEPT INT, EMP INT);
CREATE TABLE DEPT (DEPT INT, LOC INT, MGR INT);
explanation: Q1 only checks whether a given (EMP,DEPT) pair appears **at least once** in the DEPT table with LOC = 3.  Duplicates in DEPT do not change the truth-value of the IN predicate, so every qualifying EMP row is returned **once at most**.  Q2 performs an explicit join between EMP and DEPT.  If the same (DEPT,LOC,MGR) combination is stored several times in DEPT, the join produces one output row *per matching DEPT row*, so the same employee name can appear multiple times.  Because SQL result sets are bags (multisets), the two queries can therefore return different multiplicities.
counterexample_dsp: Put one employee whose (EMP,DEPT) pair appears twice in DEPT with LOC = 3.  Q1 returns the employee once, Q2 returns it twice.

q1: SELECT X.B AS XB FROM R X WHERE X.A = 5 AND X.C < 1
q2: SELECT X.B AS XB FROM R X WHERE X.A < 10
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT, B INT, C INT);
explanation: Q1 keeps only the tuples whose A = 5 and C < 1; Q2 keeps every tuple whose A < 10. Therefore any row with A < 10 but (A <> 5 OR C >= 1) appears in Q2 while being filtered-out in Q1, so the two result sets can differ.
counterexample: INSERT INTO R (A, B, C) VALUES (3, 99, 5);
counterexample_dsp: Insert one tuple with A = 3 (which is < 10) and any C value (e.g. 5). It satisfies Q2’s condition but fails Q1’s, so Q2 returns its B value while Q1 returns nothing.

q1:
SELECT 
    P.UID,
    P.UNAME,
    COALESCE(Q.CNT, 0) AS CNT
FROM (
    SELECT X.UID, X.UNAME
    FROM USER X
    WHERE X.CITY = 3
) AS P
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT Y.UID, COUNT(*) AS CNT
    FROM PICTURE Y
    WHERE Y.SIZE > 1000000
    GROUP BY Y.UID
) AS Q
USING (UID);
q2: SELECT X.UID AS UID, X.UNAME AS UNAME, COUNT(*) AS CNT FROM USER X, PICTURE Y WHERE X.UID = Y.UID AND Y.SIZE > 1000000 AND X.CITY = 3 GROUP BY X.UID, X.UNAME
schema:
CREATE TABLE USER (UID INT, UNAME INT, CITY INT);
CREATE TABLE PICTURE (UID INT, SIZE INT);
explanation: Q1 keeps **all users from CITY = 3** and LEFT-JOINs them with the count of their big pictures, converting the missing side to 0. Q2, instead, does an INNER join between USER and PICTURE first (only rows where SIZE > 1 000 000 survive) and then groups. Therefore a user who has no picture larger than 1 000 000 bytes appears in Q1 with CNT = 0 but is completely absent from Q2.
counterexample_dsp: User 1 lives in city 3 but has only a small picture (size below the limit). Q1 shows that user with CNT = 0, while Q2 returns no rows at all.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.USRUID AS XID, X.USRNAME AS XNAME FROM USR X, PIC U, PIC V, PIC W WHERE X.USRUID = U.PICUID AND X.USRUID = V.PICUID AND X.USRUID = W.PICUID AND W.PICSIZE = V.PICSIZE AND U.PICSIZE < 500000 and V.PICSIZE >= 500000
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.USRUID AS XID, X.USRNAME AS XNAME FROM USR X, PIC U, PIC V WHERE X.USRUID = U.PICUID AND X.USRUID = V.PICUID AND U.PICSIZE < 500000 and V.PICSIZE >= 500000
schema:
CREATE TABLE USR (USRUID INT, USRNAME VARCHAR);
CREATE TABLE PIC (PICUID INT, PICSIZE INT);
explanation: After analysing the predicates of both queries we see that they are logically identical.  Q2 only needs a photo U of the user that is < 500 000 and a photo V of the same user that is ≥ 500 000.  Q1 needs exactly the same two photos (U and V) and in addition a third table alias W that must have the same user id as V and the same size as V.  Such a row W is always available by simply letting W be the very same physical row that V already represents – SQL allows two different aliases to refer to the same underlying row.  Therefore every user that satisfies Q2 automatically satisfies Q1 (choose W = V), and vice-versa.  Hence the result sets are always identical and no counter-example can exist.
counterexample_dsp: No database contents can make the two queries return different results because the extra self-join in Q1 never imposes an additional constraint that cannot be met by the row already chosen for alias V.

q1: SELECT X.PNUM AS XP FROM PARTS X WHERE (X.PNUM, X.QOH) IN (SELECT Y.PNUM, COUNT(Y.SHIPDATE) AS CNT FROM SUPPLY Y WHERE Y.SHIPDATE < 10)
q2: SELECT X.PNUM AS XP FROM PARTS X, (SELECT Y.PNUM AS SUPPNUM, COUNT(Y.SHIPDATE) AS CT FROM SUPPLY Y WHERE Y.SHIPDATE < 10 GROUP BY Y.PNUM) TEMP WHERE X.QOH = TEMP.CT AND X.PNUM = TEMP.SUPPNUM
schema:
CREATE TABLE PARTS (PNUM INT, QOH INT);
CREATE TABLE SUPPLY (PNUM INT, SHIPDATE INT);
explanation: Q1 does not contain a GROUP BY although it selects both Y.PNUM (a non-aggregated column) and the aggregate COUNT(Y.SHIPDATE).  In systems that tolerate this it produces exactly ONE row: ( some-arbitrary-PNUM , total_count_of_rows_with_shipdate<10 ).  Q2, on the other hand, groups by Y.PNUM, so it produces ONE row PER part number: ( that_part’s_PNUM , count_for_that_part ).  Consequently Q1 compares every row of PARTS to a single total count, whereas Q2 compares a part only to its own individual count.  If no part happens to have that global total as its QOH, Q1 returns nothing while Q2 can still return matching parts – proving the two queries are not equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: Three supply shipments are recorded: two for part #1 and one for part #2, all with SHIPDATE < 10.  Hence the global count is 3, while the per-part counts are 2 and 1.  The PARTS table is populated so that each part’s QOH equals its own count (2 for part #1, 1 for part #2) and **no** part has QOH = 3.  Q2 therefore returns both parts, whereas Q1 returns an empty set because no (PNUM,QOH) pair equals ( arbitrary_PNUM , 3 ).

q1: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP X WHERE (X.EMP, X.DEPT) IN (SELECT Y.MGR, Y.DEPT FROM DEPT Y WHERE Y.LOC = 3)
q2: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP X
schema:
CREATE TABLE EMP (NAME INT, DEPT INT, EMP INT);
CREATE TABLE DEPT (DEPT INT, LOC INT, MGR INT);
explanation: Q1 applies a filter: it only keeps those EMP rows whose (EMP,DEPT) pair appears in the DEPT table for departments located in LOC = 3. Q2 has no such filter and therefore always returns every row in EMP. Whenever at least one employee fails that condition, the result sets diverge.
counterexample_dsp: EMP contains two employees (emp-ids 1 and 2) in department 10. DEPT shows that only emp-id 1 manages a department located at 3. Thus Q1 returns only the first employee, while Q2 returns both.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS AX FROM A X, B Y WHERE X.YA = Y.YB
q2:
SELECT X.X AS AX
FROM A X, A Y, B Z
WHERE X.X = Y.X
  AND X.YA = Z.YB

UNION ALL

SELECT 1 AS AX
FROM A X
WHERE 1 = 0;
schema:
CREATE TABLE A (X INT, YA INT);
CREATE TABLE B (YB INT);
explanation: Q1 keeps only one copy of every matching X because it uses SELECT DISTINCT, while Q2 keeps every copy generated by the join and therefore can return the same X many times.  The extra self-join of table A in Q2 (aliases X and Y) multiplies the number of rows, and because no DISTINCT is applied the duplicates survive, so the multiset results differ.
counterexample_dsp: Two rows in A share the same X value.  Only one of them matches a row in B on YA=YB.  Q1 therefore returns one row (5).  Q2’s self-join produces two rows (5,5) because the matching A row can pair with each of the two A rows that have X=5, so Q2 returns the value 5 twice.

q1: SELECT X.X AS AX FROM A X WHERE X.YX = 'HELLO'
q2: SELECT X.X AS AX FROM A X WHERE X.YX = 'HELLO HI'
schema: CREATE TABLE A (X INT, YA INT, YX VARCHAR);
explanation: The two queries filter on different literal values in column A.YX. Q1 keeps rows where YX = 'HELLO', while Q2 keeps rows where YX = 'HELLO HI'. If the table contains at least one row with one of those values and not the other, the result sets will differ.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO A (X, YA, YX) VALUES (1, 10, 'HELLO');
INSERT INTO A (X, YA, YX) VALUES (2, 20, 'HELLO HI');
counterexample_dsp: Insert one row whose YX is exactly 'HELLO' and another whose YX is exactly 'HELLO HI'. Q1 will return the X value of the first row (1); Q2 will return the X value of the second row (2).

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS X FROM R1 X, R2 Y WHERE X.Y = Y.Y AND X.X = 1
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS X FROM R1 X, R1 Y, R2 Z WHERE X.X = Y.X AND X.Y = Z.Y AND X.X = 1
schema:
CREATE TABLE R1 (X INT, Y INT);
CREATE TABLE R2 (Y INT);
explanation: After analysing the two queries it turns out that they are, in fact, equivalent.  Both need (and only need) a row in R1 with X = 1 whose Y–value can be matched by some row in R2.   The extra self-join to R1 that appears in Q2 ( alias Y ) does not add any further restriction: the same R1 row used for alias X can also be used for alias Y, so the additional predicate X.X = Y.X is automatically satisfied whenever the first condition (X.X = 1) is satisfied.  Consequently, whenever Q1 returns 1, Q2 also returns 1, and whenever Q1 returns nothing, Q2 also returns nothing.  Therefore there is no database state that can make their result sets differ, and no counter-example can be constructed.
counterexample_dsp: No counter-example exists because the queries are logically equivalent for every possible instance of the given schema.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM R X WHERE X.A1 = X.A2 AND X.A2 = X.A3
q2: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM R X WHERE X.A1 = X.A2 AND X.A1 = X.A3
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A1 INT, A2 INT, A3 INT);
explanation: Q1 requires (A1 = A2) AND (A2 = A3); Q2 requires (A1 = A2) AND (A1 = A3).  In SQL-92 three-valued logic, the only way for either query to return a row is for all referenced comparisons to evaluate to TRUE.  If (A1 = A2) is TRUE and (A2 = A3) is TRUE, then A1, A2 and A3 must all be the same non-NULL integer value, which automatically makes (A1 = A3) TRUE as well.  Conversely, if (A1 = A2) and (A1 = A3) are TRUE, then (A2 = A3) is necessarily TRUE.  Therefore the truth sets of the two predicates coincide for every possible tuple and both queries (after DISTINCT) always return exactly the same rows.  Hence no counterexample exists.
counterexample_dsp: Impossible – the predicates are logically equivalent for INT columns (including NULL handling), so there is no data that makes the result sets differ.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.* FROM R X, R Y
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.* FROM R X
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: The two queries are logically equivalent.  Q1 forms a Cartesian product R×R, then projects only the columns coming from the first copy (X.*) and removes duplicates with DISTINCT.  For every row x in R, there is at least one matching y in R whenever the table is non-empty, so x will appear in Q1’s result.  If R is empty, both queries return the empty set.  Hence for every possible contents of R the two result sets are identical.
counterexample_dsp: No data configuration can make the result sets differ, so no counter-example table can be produced.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT Y.A AS A FROM R X, R Y WHERE X.A = Y.A
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.A AS A FROM R X
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT);
explanation: Q1 compares X.A = Y.A inside the WHERE clause.  Because in SQL the predicate NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN (not TRUE), every join-pair that contains a NULL in either X.A or Y.A is filtered out.  Therefore Q1 never returns the value NULL.  Q2 simply projects A with DISTINCT and therefore does return NULL when it is present in the table.  Hence the two queries differ whenever column R.A contains at least one NULL.
counterexample: INSERT INTO R (A) VALUES (NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Insert one row whose A is NULL.  Q1 returns no rows, while Q2 returns one row with A = NULL.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT Y.A1 AS A1, Y.A2 AS A2 FROM R X, R Y WHERE X.A1 = Y.A1 AND X.A2 = Y.A2
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.A1 AS A1, X.A2 AS A2 FROM R X
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A1 INT, A2 INT);
explanation: The self-join in Q1 compares columns with the = operator.  In SQL, NULL is never equal to NULL, so any row that contains a NULL in A1 or A2 will fail the join condition and be filtered out.  Q2 does no such comparison; it simply projects the distinct values that exist in R, keeping rows that contain NULLs.  Therefore, whenever R holds at least one row whose A1 or A2 is NULL, Q1 omits that row while Q2 returns it.
counterexample: INSERT INTO R (A1, A2) VALUES (NULL, 1);
counterexample_dsp: Add one row whose join columns contain a NULL.  That row survives Q2 but is discarded by Q1 because NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN (not TRUE).

q1: SELECT X.A, SUM(X.A + X.B) FROM R X GROUP BY X.A
q2: SELECT Y.A, SUM(Y.A + Y.B) FROM R Y GROUP BY Y.A
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT, B INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are textually the same query except for the correlation name (alias) used for table R (X vs Y). Alias names have no influence on the semantics of the query: both statements group by column A of table R and compute SUM(A+B) for each such group. Therefore, for every possible database instance they always return identical result sets. No structural element (filter, join, NULL‐handling nuance, etc.) exists that could make them diverge.
counterexample_dsp: Because the two queries are semantically identical, **no counter-example data can make them return different results**.

q1: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 50) Y WHERE Y.X < 200
q2: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X < 200) Y WHERE Y.X > 50
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Q1 first keeps rows with X > 50 and then discards any of those that are >= 200. Q2 first keeps rows with X < 200 and then discards any of those that are <= 50. In ordinary SQL (3-valued logic, no user-defined functions, no side effects) a row is returned only if it satisfies BOTH filters, i.e. 50 < X < 200. The order in which the two independent filters are applied does not matter, so the result sets are always identical.
counterexample_dsp: Because the predicates are commutative (AND), there is no legal instance of table R that can make one query return a row the other does not. Hence no counter-example exists.

q1: SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 50 AND X.X < 200
q2: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 50) Y WHERE Y.X < 200
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Both queries apply exactly the same two predicates (X > 50 and X < 200) to the same table. Q2 just splits the predicates across an inner and an outer WHERE clause, but the logical conjunction of the two conditions is identical to the single conjunctive predicate in Q1. No SQL features that could introduce divergence (NULL handling, duplicates, ordering, joins, aggregation, etc.) are used differently, so the result sets are always identical.
counterexample_dsp: No counter-example exists – the queries are equivalent for every possible instance of table R that respects the schema constraints.

q1: SELECT COUNT(*) AS A FROM R X
q2: SELECT COUNT(Y.B) FROM R Y
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT, B INT);
explanation: COUNT(*) counts every row, regardless of NULLs in any column. COUNT(Y.B) only counts rows where column B is NOT NULL. Therefore, if at least one row has B = NULL, Q1 will count it while Q2 will ignore it, giving different results.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO R (A, B) VALUES (1, NULL);
INSERT INTO R (A, B) VALUES (2, 10);
counterexample_dsp: Insert one row whose B is NULL (or a mix of NULL and non-NULL). Q1 will include that row in its total, Q2 will not.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 50 OR X.X < 200
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: No counter-example exists.  For every non-NULL value of R.X either (X > 50) or (X < 200) – in fact at least one of them is always TRUE – therefore Q1 returns every non-NULL row of R (duplicates removed by DISTINCT).  Q2 separately selects the rows where X > 50 and where X < 200, UNION ALLs them, and finally applies DISTINCT, which also yields every non-NULL row of R once.  NULLs are excluded by both queries because both comparisons return UNKNOWN for NULL.  Hence the result sets of Q1 and Q2 are identical for every possible database instance.
counterexample_dsp: Impossible – the queries are equivalent for all data, so no database can make them differ.

q1: SELECT DEPT.NAME AS DNAME, COUNT(*) AS C FROM DEPT AS DEPT GROUP BY DEPT.NAME HAVING DEPT.NAME = 10
q2: SELECT T2.DNAME, T2.CNT AS C FROM (SELECT DEPT0.NAME AS DNAME, COUNT(*) AS CNT FROM DEPT AS DEPT0 GROUP BY DEPT0.NAME) AS T2 WHERE T2.DNAME = 10
schema: CREATE TABLE DEPT (DEPTNO INT, NAME INT);
explanation: After analysing grouping, filtering and NULL–handling it turns out that both queries do the very same thing: they aggregate DEPT rows by NAME, count how many belong to each NAME and finally keep only the group whose NAME equals the literal 10.  Because the sequence of operations (GROUP BY → filter on NAME = 10) is identical, every possible database state yields identical result sets; therefore the two queries are equivalent and no counter-example exists.
counterexample: -- (no INSERTs, because no counterexample is possible)
counterexample_dsp: Impossible – any data you insert will make Q1 and Q2 return the same rows.  Hence no counterexample database can be constructed.

q1: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 0) Y WHERE Y.X > 0
q2: SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 0
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Q1 filters the table R for rows with X>0 inside a derived table, then **re-applies the exact same filter** on that derived table. Q2 performs the very same single filter directly on R. Because there is no DISTINCT, aggregation, join, or NULL-handling construct that could alter the result between the two identical predicates, the two queries always return exactly the same set of rows for every possible instance of table R. Hence they are logically equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: No counter-example exists – there is no legal instance of table R that can make the two queries diverge.

q1: SELECT * FROM A X WHERE X.C IN (SELECT Y.C FROM A Y)
q2: SELECT * FROM A X
schema: CREATE TABLE A (C INT);
explanation: Q1 keeps only those rows whose value X.C satisfies the predicate X.C IN ( … ). For a row where X.C is NULL the comparison "NULL IN (sub-query)" is UNKNOWN, therefore the WHERE filter rejects that row. Q2 has no such filter and returns every row. Hence, as soon as table A contains at least one NULL in column C, the two queries produce different results.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO A (C) VALUES (NULL);
INSERT INTO A (C) VALUES (1);
counterexample_dsp: Insert one row with C = NULL (filtered out by Q1) and another with a non-NULL value (returned by both queries).

q1: SELECT X.A1 AS A1, X.A2 AS A2, Y.B1 AS B1, Y.B2 AS B2 FROM A X, B Y WHERE X.A1 = Y.B1
q2: SELECT Y.A1 AS A1, Y.A2 AS A2, X.B1 AS B1, X.B2 AS B2 FROM B X, A Y WHERE Y.A1 = X.B1
schema:
CREATE TABLE A (A1 INT, A2 INT);
CREATE TABLE B (B1 INT, B2 INT);
explanation: No matter what data are stored in A and B, both queries perform exactly the same inner-join condition (A.A1 = B.B1) and project the same four columns in the same order (A.A1, A.A2, B.B1, B.B2).  The only visible difference is the choice of aliases (X vs. Y), which does not affect the result set.  Consequently the two queries are logically equivalent and there exists no database instance that can make their outputs differ.
counterexample_dsp: Impossible – the queries are equivalent, so every legal dataset gives identical results.

q1: SELECT * FROM R1 X, (SELECT * FROM R2 UNION ALL SELECT * FROM R3) Y
explanation: Q1 first forms the multiset R2∪ALL R3 and then takes the cartesian product with R1.  Q2 takes the cartesian products R1×R2 and R1×R3 separately and then unions-all the two results.  Because the cartesian product distributes over UNION ALL under multiset semantics, the two expressions always yield the same rows with the same multiplicities (and the same column order/names chosen from the first SELECT list).  Hence the queries are logically equivalent for every possible database; no data can make them differ.
counterexample_dsp: Not possible – the queries are equivalent, so there is no dataset that would make their results diverge.

q1: SELECT X.B AS XB, Y.B AS YB FROM R1 X, R2 Y
q2: SELECT X1.XB AS XB, Y1.YB AS YB FROM (SELECT X.B AS XB FROM R1 X) X1, (SELECT Y.B AS YB FROM R2 Y) Y1
schema:
CREATE TABLE R1 (A INT, B INT);
CREATE TABLE R2 (A INT, B INT);
explanation: After analyzing the two queries we see that both of them do exactly the same thing: they form the Cartesian product between R1 and R2 and then project the B-column from each side.  Q2 only wraps each base table into a trivial sub-query ("SELECT B …") but does not add DISTINCT, filters, aggregation, or any other construct that might alter multiplicities or NULL treatment.  Therefore every row that Q1 produces is produced by Q2 and vice-versa with identical duplicates and NULLs preserved.  Because the semantics are identical for every possible database state, no counter-example can be constructed.
counterexample_dsp: Not applicable – the queries are equivalent, so there exists no data instance on which they diverge.

q1: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R UNION ALL SELECT * FROM S) X
schema:
CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
CREATE TABLE S (X INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 both simply return every row from table R followed by every row from table S using UNION ALL (which preserves duplicates). The outer SELECT in Q1 does not add any filtering, aggregation or other operation that could change the multiset of rows. Therefore, the two queries always yield the same result set (ignoring ordering, which SQL does not guarantee without ORDER BY).
counterexample_dsp: No data can make them differ – the queries are logically equivalent for every possible population of tables R and S.

q1: SELECT * FROM A X, (SELECT * FROM B Y WHERE Y.X < 100) Z WHERE X.X = Z.X
q2: SELECT * FROM A X, B Y WHERE X.X = Y.X AND Y.X < 100
schema:
CREATE TABLE A (X INT);
CREATE TABLE B (X INT);
explanation: The two queries are logically identical: both return every pair (A.X, B.X) such that the values are equal and B.X is below 100.  Q1 first builds a derived table Z that already contains only the B-rows with X<100 and then joins A with Z on equality; Q2 performs the same equality join against B and applies the very same predicate (Y.X<100) in the WHERE clause.  Because the sub-query in Q1 does not add DISTINCT, aggregation, or any other operation that could change multiplicities, and because both queries use plain inner joins, duplicates and NULL semantics are preserved in exactly the same way.  Hence, for every possible content of A and B, the two result sets (including row counts and column order) coincide.
counterexample_dsp: Such a counterexample does not exist – the queries are equivalent for all databases that respect the given schema.

q1: SELECT X.A AS A FROM X X, Y Y WHERE X.K = Y.K
q2: SELECT X1.A AS X1A FROM (SELECT X.A AS A, X.K AS K FROM X X) X1, Y Y WHERE X1.K = Y.K
schema:
CREATE TABLE X (A INT, K INT);
CREATE TABLE Y (A INT, K INT);
explanation: Both queries return the same row-values, but the SELECT-list is aliased differently.  Q1 labels the result column “A”, while Q2 labels it “X1A”.  Because the column name is part of the query result’s observable output, the two queries are **not** equivalent – their schemas differ even when the data contained in the rows is identical.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO X (A, K) VALUES (1, 1);
INSERT INTO Y (A, K) VALUES (99, 1);
counterexample_dsp: Any non-empty data set is sufficient; the difference is visible even with one matching row because the column label produced by Q1 is A, whereas Q2 produces X1A.

q1: SELECT * FROM R1 X, (SELECT * FROM R2 Y WHERE Y.X > 0) Z
q2: SELECT * FROM R1 X, R2 Y WHERE Y.X > 0
schema:
CREATE TABLE R1 (X INT);
CREATE TABLE R2 (X INT);
explanation: Q1 first filters R2 for the condition Y.X > 0 and then performs a Cartesian product with every row of R1. Q2 performs the Cartesian product of R1 and R2 first and afterwards applies the very same filter Y.X > 0. Because the predicate only references columns of R2, the order in which the filter and the (un-conditioned) join are executed does not change the resulting set of rows: every qualifying row from R2 is combined with every row from R1 in either case. Therefore the two statements are logically equivalent and will always return exactly the same result for any database satisfying the given schema.
counterexample: -- (none: the queries are equivalent, so no INSERTs can make them differ)
counterexample_dsp: No counter-example can be constructed – the queries are equivalent for all possible data.

q1: SELECT X.A + X.B, X.A/X.B AS A FROM R X
q2: SELECT Y.A + Y.B, Y.A/Y.B AS A FROM R Y
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT, B INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are textually identical except for the table-alias name (X versus Y). They select the same two expressions from the same single table R. Because the SQL language treats table aliases merely as local identifiers, changing X to Y has no impact on semantics. Consequently, for every possible state of table R the result multisets (including column names, order, duplicates, NULL handling, errors, etc.) are identical. Therefore no database instance can make them diverge.
counterexample_dsp: Impossible – there is no legal instance of R that would let the two queries return different results.

q1: SELECT * FROM A X UNION ALL SELECT * FROM A X WHERE FALSE
q2: SELECT * FROM A X
schema: CREATE TABLE A (X INT);
explanation: Q1’s second SELECT is guarded by WHERE FALSE, so it never contributes any rows. The UNION ALL therefore just returns the rows coming from the first SELECT, i.e. every row in table A. Q2 also returns every row in table A. Hence, for every possible population of table A, the two result-multisets are identical.
counterexample_dsp: No data can make the queries differ; they are logically equivalent.

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(C.CREDITS) > 10 AND COUNT(DISTINCT C.CREDITS) > 5
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(C.CREDITS) > 10 AND COUNT(DISTINCT C.CREDITS) > 8
explanation: Both queries group courses by department and keep only those groups where the total number of credits is larger than 10.  The difference is the second HAVING-clause predicate: Q1 keeps departments that have more than 5 distinct credit values, while Q2 requires more than 8.  Therefore, a department that has 6–8 different credit amounts (and whose credits sum to > 10) will appear in Q1 but be filtered out in Q2.
counterexample_dsp: Create one department and six courses in it whose credit values are 1–6.  The group’s SUM(credits)=21 (>10) and COUNT(DISTINCT credits)=6 (>5 but not >8).  Hence Q1 returns that department whereas Q2 returns nothing.

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, AVG(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING AVG(I.SALARY)>50000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)=4
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, AVG(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING AVG(I.SALARY)>50000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)>4
explanation: The two queries are identical except for the HAVING predicate on COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY).  Q1 keeps groups whose number of distinct salaries is exactly 4, while Q2 keeps groups whose number of distinct salaries is greater than 4.  Therefore any department that has exactly four distinct instructor salaries (and an average salary > 50 000) will appear in Q1 but will be filtered out by Q2.
counterexample_dsp: Create one department that owns one course.  Add exactly four instructors in that department with distinct salaries (all > 50 000).  Add one TEACHES row so the joins are non-empty.  For that department the AVG salary is > 50 000 and COUNT(DISTINCT salary) = 4, so Q1 returns the row and Q2 does not.

q1: SELECT STUDENT.ID FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT NATURAL JOIN STUDENT NATURAL JOIN TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY STUDENT.ID,STUDENT.DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(DEPT_NAME) >= 2
q2: SELECT STUDENT.ID FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT NATURAL JOIN STUDENT NATURAL JOIN TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY STUDENT.ID HAVING COUNT(DEPT_NAME) >= 2
explanation: Q1 groups by (STUDENT.ID , STUDENT.DEPT_NAME) while Q2 groups only by STUDENT.ID.  If the same student-id appears under two different department names (possible because the schema declares no primary-key or foreign-key constraints on STUDENT.ID), rows for that student are split into two separate groups in Q1 but are merged into one group in Q2.  With two different departments the merged group in Q2 reaches COUNT(DEPT_NAME)=2 and passes the HAVING filter, whereas each smaller group in Q1 has COUNT(DEPT_NAME)=1 and is filtered out.  Hence the two queries can return different result sets.
counterexample_dsp: Student 1 is stored twice, once in dept 10 and once in dept 20, and takes one course offered by each of those departments.  This produces two joined rows.  Q2 merges them (count=2) and returns ID 1, Q1 keeps them in two groups (count=1 each) and returns nothing.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS = (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT WHERE TITLE='CS' GROUP BY DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT COURSE_ID)>4)
q2: SELECT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS = (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT WHERE TITLE='CS' GROUP BY DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT COURSE_ID)>4)
explanation: The only syntactic difference between Q1 and Q2 is the keyword DISTINCT that Q1 applies to the final projection list.  Q1 therefore eliminates duplicate department-names that satisfy the WHERE clause, while Q2 returns one row for every qualifying tuple in COURSE.  If two or more different COURSE rows of the same department have the credit value produced by the sub-query, Q2 will emit that department more than once, whereas Q1 will report it once.  Hence the queries are not equivalent whenever such duplicates exist.
counterexample_dsp: The sub-query is made to return the value 5 by creating one department that offers >4 CS courses whose maximum credit is 5.  Two of those courses have 5 credits, so the outer WHERE clause is true for two rows with the same DEPT_NAME.  Q1 keeps only one of them (because of DISTINCT); Q2 returns both.

q1: SELECT STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME FROM STUDENT JOIN (SELECT TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR FROM TAKES JOIN SECTION AS S ON TAKES.COURSE_ID = S.COURSE_ID AND TAKES.SEC_ID = S.SEC_ID GROUP BY TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR HAVING COUNT(S.TIME_SLOT_ID) > 1) AS A ON STUDENT.ID = A.ID GROUP BY STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2
q2: SELECT STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME FROM STUDENT JOIN (SELECT TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR FROM TAKES JOIN SECTION AS S ON TAKES.COURSE_ID = S.COURSE_ID AND TAKES.SEC_ID = S.SEC_ID GROUP BY TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR HAVING SUM(S.TIME_SLOT_ID) > 1) AS A ON STUDENT.ID = A.ID GROUP BY STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2
explanation: Although the sub-queries are different (COUNT vs. SUM on TIME_SLOT_ID), the surrounding query makes the difference unreachable. After the JOIN, the result is grouped by (STUDENT.ID , STUDENT.NAME). Inside such a group the value of STUDENT.ID is fixed, therefore COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) is either 1 (if the ID is NOT NULL) or 0 (if it is NULL). It can never exceed 2, so the HAVING clause (COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2) is impossible to satisfy. Consequently both Q1 and Q2 always return the empty result set for every possible database state – they are equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: No specific data (or even an empty database) suffices, because both queries always return an empty set. Hence a counter-example cannot exist.

q1: SELECT SUM(T) AS SU FROM (SELECT YEAR AS T FROM TEACHES NATURAL JOIN INSTRUCTOR GROUP BY YEAR, COURSE_ID HAVING COUNT(ID)>4) AS TEMP GROUP BY T
q2: SELECT SUM(T) AS SU FROM (SELECT YEAR AS T FROM TEACHES NATURAL JOIN INSTRUCTOR GROUP BY YEAR HAVING COUNT(ID)>4) AS TEMP GROUP BY T
explanation: Inside the inner sub-query Q1 groups by (YEAR , COURSE_ID) while Q2 groups only by YEAR.  Therefore, if in the same YEAR two (or more) different COURSE_ID groups individually have >4 matching TEACHES rows, Q1 will return that YEAR once for every qualifying course, whereas Q2 will return the YEAR only once.  The outer query then sums the duplicated YEAR values, so Q1 and Q2 return different sums.
counterexample_dsp: In 2020 instructor 1 teaches two different courses (100 and 200), five sections each.  Each (YEAR , COURSE_ID) combination has 5 rows (count(ID)=5) so both qualify the HAVING clause. Q1 therefore sees the year 2020 twice and sums 2020+2020=4040, while Q2 sees it once and returns 2020.

q1: WITH S AS (SELECT ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR FROM TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR HAVING COUNT(TIME_SLOT_ID)>4) SELECT DISTINCT ID,NAME FROM S NATURAL JOIN STUDENT
q2: WITH S AS (SELECT ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR FROM TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR HAVING COUNT(TIME_SLOT_ID)>5) SELECT DISTINCT ID,NAME FROM S NATURAL JOIN STUDENT
explanation: The two queries differ only in the HAVING-predicate of the inner grouping:  Q1 keeps groups with COUNT(time_slot_id) > 4, while Q2 keeps groups with COUNT(time_slot_id) > 5.  Therefore a group that contains exactly 5 matching rows (same student id, same time-slot, same year) is returned by Q1 but filtered out by Q2; the final NATURAL JOIN with STUDENT then makes the result sets different.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO COURSE  (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES
  (1,0,0,3), (2,0,0,3), (3,0,0,3), (4,0,0,3), (5,0,0,3);

INSERT INTO SECTION (COURSE_ID, SEC_ID, YEAR, BUILDING, ROOM_NUMBER, TIME_SLOT_ID) VALUES
  (1,1,2023,0,0,100),
  (2,2,2023,0,0,100),
  (3,3,2023,0,0,100),
  (4,4,2023,0,0,100),
  (5,5,2023,0,0,100);

INSERT INTO STUDENT (ID, NAME, DEPT_NAME, TOT_CRED) VALUES
  (1,100,10,0);

INSERT INTO TAKES (ID, COURSE_ID, SEC_ID, YEAR, GRADE) VALUES
  (1,1,1,2023,NULL),
  (1,2,2,2023,NULL),
  (1,3,3,2023,NULL),
  (1,4,4,2023,NULL),
  (1,5,5,2023,NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Student 1 is registered (TAKES) in exactly five different sections that all occur in the same year (2023) and have the same TIME_SLOT_ID (100).  These five rows satisfy COUNT=5, so Q1 returns the student, but Q2 (requiring COUNT>5) returns no row.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE JOIN (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) AS MAX_CREDITS FROM COURSE) AS A ON COURSE.CREDITS = A.MAX_CREDITS
q2: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE JOIN (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) AS MAX_CREDITS FROM COURSE GROUP BY DEPT_NAME) AS A ON COURSE.CREDITS = A.MAX_CREDITS
explanation: Q1 first finds the single, global maximum CREDITS value in COURSE and returns the departments of courses that have exactly that value. Q2, however, finds the maximum CREDITS value separately inside every department (GROUP BY DEPT_NAME). It then keeps only the numeric maxima, forgets which department they belonged to, and matches every course whose CREDITS equals *any* of those numbers. Therefore Q2 can return departments whose own maximum-credit course is **smaller** than the global maximum, whereas Q1 never will. The difference appears as soon as at least one department has its highest-credit course below the overall maximum.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES
  (1, 101, 10, 4),  -- dept 10, global max credits
  (2, 102, 10, 2),
  (3, 201, 20, 3),  -- dept 20’s own max credits (below global max)
  (4, 202, 20, 1);
counterexample_dsp: Department 10 has a 4-credit course (the global maximum). Department 20’s highest-credit course is 3. Q1 returns only department 10; Q2 returns both departments because 3 is one of the per-department maxima produced by its subquery.

q1: SELECT C.NAME FROM CARRIERS AS C JOIN FLIGHTS AS F ON C.CID = F.CARRIER_ID GROUP BY C.NAME, F.YEAR, F.MONTH_ID, F.DAY_OF_MONTH HAVING COUNT(F.FID) > 1000
q2: SELECT C.NAME FROM CARRIERS AS C JOIN FLIGHTS AS F ON C.CID = F.CARRIER_ID GROUP BY C.NAME, F.DAY_OF_MONTH HAVING COUNT(C.CID) > 1000
explanation: Q1 counts the number of flights (non-NULL F.FID values) for every combination of carrier name, year, month and day-of-month.  Q2, in contrast, counts how many joined rows (via C.CID) exist for every combination of carrier name and day-of-month only.  Because the grouping keys are different, the same rows can be split into many small groups in Q1 but stay in one big group in Q2.  By adding many duplicate CARRIERS rows (which multiplies the join result) we can make the big group exceed 1000 rows while every small group stays below that threshold, so Q2 returns the carrier name and Q1 does not.
counterexample_dsp: 101 identical CARRIERS rows (same CID and NAME) and 10 FLIGHTS spread over 10 different months but on the same day-of-month.  After the join there are 101×10 = 1 010 rows for that (name,day) pair (>1000), yet only 101 rows per (name,year,month,day) combination (≤1000).  Hence Q2 returns the carrier name whereas Q1 returns nothing.

q1: SELECT C.NAME FROM CARRIERS AS C JOIN FLIGHTS AS F ON C.CID = F.CARRIER_ID GROUP BY C.CID, C.NAME, F.YEAR, F.MONTH_ID, F.DAY_OF_MONTH HAVING COUNT(F.FID) > 1000
q2: SELECT C.NAME FROM CARRIERS AS C JOIN FLIGHTS AS F ON C.CID = F.CARRIER_ID GROUP BY C.NAME, F.DAY_OF_MONTH HAVING COUNT(F.FID) > 1000
explanation: Both queries count how many flight-rows are associated with a carrier name, but they aggregate on different columns.  Q1 splits the data by C.CID, YEAR, MONTH_ID and DAY_OF_MONTH, while Q2 only uses NAME and DAY_OF_MONTH.  Therefore rows that fall into different months (or belong to different carrier IDs that share the same name) are counted in separate groups by Q1 but are merged together by Q2.  If no single (CID,year,month,day) group exceeds 1 000 rows, Q1 returns nothing, while Q2 can still exceed the threshold after it merges the same name across months and will return that name.
counterexample_dsp: One carrier (CID=1, NAME='X') has 512 flights on day 1 of month 1 and another 512 flights on day 1 of month 2 (total 1 024 flights).  Any individual (CID,year,month,day) combination has only 512 flights (< 1 001) so Q1 returns no rows, but Q2 aggregates both months together (name ‘X’, day 1) and gets 1 024 flights (> 1 000), therefore it returns ‘X’.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT F.ORIGIN_CITY, F.DEST_CITY, F.ACTUAL_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS F JOIN (SELECT A.ORIGIN_CITY, MAX(A.ACTUAL_TIME) AS MAX_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS A GROUP BY A.ORIGIN_CITY) AS X ON F.ORIGIN_CITY = X.ORIGIN_CITY AND F.ACTUAL_TIME = X.MAX_TIME
q2: SELECT S.ORIGIN_CITY, F2.DEST_CITY, MAX(F2.ACTUAL_TIME) FROM (SELECT F1.ORIGIN_CITY, MAX(F1.ACTUAL_TIME) AS MAX_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS F1 GROUP BY F1.ORIGIN_CITY) AS S JOIN FLIGHTS AS F2 ON S.ORIGIN_CITY = F2.ORIGIN_CITY AND F2.ACTUAL_TIME = S.MAX_TIME GROUP BY S.ORIGIN_CITY, F2.DEST_CITY
explanation: After analysing the two statements we find that they are actually equivalent for every possible database state.  Both queries (1) compute, for every origin–city, the maximum ACTUAL_TIME, (2) keep only those flight rows whose ACTUAL_TIME equals that per-origin maximum and (3) report one result row per (origin_city , dest_city) pair together with that common maximum time.  Q1 removes duplicates with DISTINCT, while Q2 first keeps the duplicates produced by the join and then collapses them with GROUP BY/ MAX – but in both cases the same set of rows survives, so no database can make the outputs diverge.
counterexample_dsp: Because the two queries are equivalent, there exists no counter-example that would yield different result sets.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT F.ORIGIN_CITY, F.DEST_CITY, F.ACTUAL_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS F JOIN (SELECT A.ORIGIN_CITY, MAX(A.ACTUAL_TIME) AS MAX_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS A GROUP BY A.ORIGIN_CITY) AS X ON F.ORIGIN_CITY = X.ORIGIN_CITY AND F.ACTUAL_TIME = X.MAX_TIME
q2: SELECT P.ORIGIN_CITY, P.DEST_CITY, P.ACTUAL_TIME FROM (SELECT F1.ORIGIN_CITY, F1.DEST_CITY, F1.ACTUAL_TIME, MAX(F2.ACTUAL_TIME) AS MAX_ACTUAL_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS F1 JOIN FLIGHTS AS F2 ON F1.ORIGIN_CITY = F2.ORIGIN_CITY GROUP BY F1.ORIGIN_CITY, F1.DEST_CITY, F1.ACTUAL_TIME) AS P WHERE P.ACTUAL_TIME = P.MAX_ACTUAL_TIME
explanation:
After a detailed step-by-step analysis we did not find any relational situation in which Q1 and Q2 diverge.  
• Q1 keeps every flight whose ACTUAL_TIME equals the maximum ACTUAL_TIME that appears for its ORIGIN_CITY (ties are kept and duplicates are removed by DISTINCT).  
• Q2 first pairs each row F1 with every other row F2 that has the same ORIGIN_CITY, then – for every (F1) group – remembers the maximum ACTUAL_TIME that was seen in the paired F2 rows; it finally keeps the rows whose own ACTUAL_TIME equals that maximum.  
For every flight f the maximum over the F2 rows always contains f’s own ACTUAL_TIME, therefore f survives the final filter in Q2 exactly when it survives the join in Q1.  Grouping in Q2 collapses duplicates in the same way as the DISTINCT in Q1, so the two result sets are always identical.  Consequently, no counterexample (database state producing different outputs) exists.
counterexample_dsp: Not applicable – the two queries are equivalent for all possible instances of the given schema.

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(C.CREDITS)>10 AND COUNT(C.CREDITS)>5
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(C.CREDITS)>10 AND COUNT(C.CREDITS)>8
explanation:
Both queries aggregate COURSE rows per department after an inner-join with DEPARTMENT and then apply a HAVING filter.
• They both keep groups whose total credits (SUM(C.CREDITS)) are above 10.
• They diverge on the second HAVING condition: Q1 keeps groups with more than 5 rows (COUNT(C.CREDITS) > 5), whereas Q2 requires more than 8 rows (COUNT(C.CREDITS) > 8).
Therefore, a department that has 6–8 courses (sum of credits still > 10) is returned by Q1 but filtered out by Q2.
counterexample_dsp: Department 1 owns exactly 6 courses, each worth 2 credits.  Total credits = 12 (>10) and row-count = 6 (>5 but ≤8).  Hence Q1 returns the department, Q2 does not.

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(I.SALARY)>100 AND MAX(I.SALARY)<75
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(I.SALARY)>=100 AND MAX(I.SALARY)<75
explanation: The two queries differ only in the HAVING-condition that compares the aggregated salary sum: Q1 requires SUM(I.SALARY) > 100 whereas Q2 accepts SUM(I.SALARY) >= 100. Therefore a department whose instructors’ salaries add up to exactly 100 (while the maximum individual salary stays below 75) will be returned by Q2 but filtered out by Q1.
counterexample_dsp:
Department 1 has one course and two instructors whose salaries are 60 and 40. The join duplicates each instructor once (one course × two instructors) so the GROUP BY dept_name sees the salaries {60,40}.  SUM = 100 (=100) and MAX = 60 (<75).  Hence:
  • Q2 returns the row (because 100 >= 100 and 60 < 75).
  • Q1 does not return the row (because 100 is NOT > 100).

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(D.BUDGET) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(D.BUDGET)>100000 AND COUNT(D.BUDGET)>10
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(D.BUDGET) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(D.BUDGET)>100000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT D.BUDGET)>10
explanation: Both queries group the join of DEPARTMENT-COURSE-TEACHES by department.  They agree on the SUM condition (>100 000) but differ on the second HAVING clause:  Q1 uses COUNT(D.BUDGET) (every joined row), while Q2 uses COUNT(DISTINCT D.BUDGET).  If many joined rows have the same budget value, COUNT will grow while COUNT(DISTINCT) stays small, so one query can pass the HAVING test and the other fail.
counterexample_dsp: Give one department with budget 10 000, one course belonging to it and 11 TEACHES rows for that course.  The join produces 11 rows, hence SUM(BUDGET)=110 000 and COUNT=11, but COUNT(DISTINCT)=1.  Therefore Q1 returns the department (conditions 110 000>100 000 and 11>10 are true) while Q2 does not (1>10 is false).

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, AVG(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING AVG(I.SALARY)>50000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)=4
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, AVG(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING AVG(I.SALARY)>50000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)>4
explanation:
The two queries are identical except for the last predicate in the HAVING clause.
  • Q1 keeps groups whose number of DISTINCT salaries is exactly 4 (COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)=4).
  • Q2 keeps groups whose number of DISTINCT salaries is greater than 4 (COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)>4).
Therefore a department that has exactly four different instructor-salary values (and an average salary above 50 000) is returned by Q1 but filtered out by Q2.
counterexample_dsp: Department 1 has one course that is taught (so the joins succeed) and exactly four instructors with different salaries (60 000, 70 000, 80 000, 90 000).  The average salary is 75 000 (> 50 000) and the count of distinct salaries is 4, meeting Q1’s condition but not Q2’s.

q1: SELECT T.SEMESTER, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM DEPARTMENT D INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (D.BUDGET = T.YEAR + 4) INNER JOIN COURSE C ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY T.SEMESTER HAVING AVG(C.CREDITS)>2 AND COUNT(D.BUILDING)=2
q2: SELECT T.SEMESTER, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM DEPARTMENT D INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (D.BUDGET = T.YEAR + 4) INNER JOIN COURSE C ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY T.SEMESTER HAVING AVG(C.CREDITS)>2 AND COUNT(D.BUILDING)>=2
explanation: The two queries are identical except for the HAVING-clause predicate on COUNT(D.BUILDING).  Q1 keeps a semester only when the joined rows contain exactly 2 non-NULL BUILDING values, while Q2 keeps it when there are at least 2.  Therefore, any semester group that contains 3 or more joined rows (all with non-NULL BUILDING) will be returned by Q2 but filtered out by Q1.
counterexample_dsp: Create one department and one course (credits = 3).  Add three TEACHES rows for the same semester and a year whose (year + 4) matches the department’s budget.  The group for that semester has COUNT(D.BUILDING)=3 (>2) and AVG(C.CREDITS)=3 (>2).  Hence Q2 returns the row while Q1 does not.

q1: SELECT ID FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT NATURAL JOIN STUDENT NATURAL JOIN TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID,DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(DEPT_NAME) >= 2
q2: SELECT ID FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT NATURAL JOIN STUDENT NATURAL JOIN TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID HAVING COUNT(DEPT_NAME) >= 2
explanation:
The two queries differ in their GROUP BY lists.  Q1 forms groups on (ID, DEPT_NAME); Q2 groups only on ID.  If the same student ID is recorded under two different department names (data anomaly that is allowed because no key/-FK is declared), the join will produce one row for each (ID, DEPT_NAME) pair.  
• In Q2 the two rows are aggregated together, COUNT(DEPT_NAME)=2, so the ID is returned.
• In Q1 each department gets its own group, every group contains only one row, COUNT(DEPT_NAME)=1, so the ID is **not** returned.
Thus the queries are not equivalent whenever one student ID appears with at least two different DEPT_NAME values in the join result.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO DEPARTMENT (DEPT_NAME, BUILDING, BUDGET) VALUES
  (1, 100, 100000),
  (2, 200, 200000);

INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES
  (101, 1001, 1, 3),   -- course in department 1
  (102, 1002, 2, 4);   -- course in department 2

INSERT INTO SECTION (COURSE_ID, SEC_ID, YEAR, BUILDING, ROOM_NUMBER, TIME_SLOT_ID) VALUES
  (101, 1, 2023, 1, 101, 1),
  (102, 1, 2023, 1, 102, 1);

-- Same student ID appears in two different departments
INSERT INTO STUDENT (ID, NAME, DEPT_NAME, TOT_CRED) VALUES
  (10, 100, 1, 0),  -- student 10, dept 1
  (10, 200, 2, 0);  -- student 10, dept 2

-- The student takes one course in each department
INSERT INTO TAKES (ID, COURSE_ID, SEC_ID, YEAR, GRADE) VALUES
  (10, 101, 1, 2023, NULL),
  (10, 102, 1, 2023, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Student 10 is stored twice, once in department 1 and once in department 2.  He takes one course from each department.  Q2 sees two rows for ID 10 and returns it; Q1 splits them into two separate (ID, DEPT_NAME) groups and returns nothing.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS = (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT WHERE TITLE='CS' GROUP BY DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(COURSE_ID)>2)
q2: SELECT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS = (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT WHERE TITLE='CS' GROUP BY DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(COURSE_ID)>2)
explanation: Q1 adds DISTINCT on the outer-query projection while Q2 does not. If several rows in COURSE satisfy the credit condition, Q2 will return one copy of DEPT_NAME for every matching row, whereas Q1 collapses them to a single row. Therefore they are not equivalent whenever the predicate matches two or more COURSE rows that belong to the same department (or different departments that share the same credit value).
counterexample:
INSERT INTO DEPARTMENT (DEPT_NAME, BUILDING, BUDGET) VALUES
  (10, 1, 10000);

-- three courses offered by department 10; TITLE = 0 matches the literal 'CS' after implicit numeric conversion
INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES
  (1, 0, 10, 4),  -- maximal credit
  (2, 0, 10, 3),  -- lower credit
  (3, 0, 10, 4);  -- maximal credit (duplicate department row)
counterexample_dsp: Department 10 has three CS courses (TITLE value that matches the literal 'CS'). Two of those courses carry the same, maximal credit value (4). The sub-query therefore returns 4. The outer WHERE keeps the two 4-credit rows, yielding two identical DEPT_NAME values. Q1 shows the department once, Q2 shows it twice.

q1: SELECT STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME FROM STUDENT JOIN (SELECT TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR FROM TAKES JOIN SECTION AS S ON TAKES.COURSE_ID = S.COURSE_ID AND TAKES.SEC_ID = S.SEC_ID GROUP BY TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR HAVING COUNT(S.TIME_SLOT_ID) > 1) AS A ON STUDENT.ID = A.ID GROUP BY STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2
q2: SELECT STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME FROM STUDENT JOIN (SELECT TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR FROM TAKES JOIN SECTION AS S ON TAKES.COURSE_ID = S.COURSE_ID AND TAKES.SEC_ID = S.SEC_ID GROUP BY TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR HAVING SUM(S.TIME_SLOT_ID) > 1) AS A ON STUDENT.ID = A.ID GROUP BY STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2
explanation: Both statements are actually *unsatisfiable*: after the join, the outer query groups BY STUDENT.ID and STUDENT.NAME and then checks HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2.  Because STUDENT.ID is part of the GROUP-BY key, every resulting group can contain only one distinct STUDENT.ID value, so COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) is always 1 (or 0 if the id is NULL) – never larger than 2.  Consequently each query always produces the empty result set, whatever data are present.  Since the result is always the same (the empty set), no database instance can make Q1 and Q2 behave differently.
counterexample: -- any set of INSERTs would make both queries return the empty set
counterexample_dsp: Impossible – the two queries are equivalent for *all* possible databases because the outer HAVING clause cannot be satisfied.

q1: SELECT SUM(T) AS SU FROM (SELECT YEAR AS T FROM TEACHES NATURAL JOIN INSTRUCTOR GROUP BY YEAR, COURSE_ID HAVING COUNT(ID)>4) AS TEMP GROUP BY T
q2: SELECT SUM(T) AS SU FROM (SELECT YEAR AS T FROM TEACHES NATURAL JOIN INSTRUCTOR GROUP BY YEAR HAVING COUNT(ID)>4) AS TEMP GROUP BY T
explanation:
Q1 first groups by (YEAR , COURSE_ID) and keeps every (YEAR , COURSE_ID) combination that has more than 4 joined rows, then it only projects YEAR.  If several different COURSE_ID of the same YEAR satisfy the HAVING condition, that YEAR will appear several times in the sub-query.  The outer query groups again by YEAR (T) and sums these duplicates, so every qualifying COURSE_ID makes the value YEAR count once more.  

Q2 groups only by YEAR, therefore each YEAR can appear at most once.  Consequently, when a single YEAR contains two (or more) qualifying COURSE_ID, Q1 will add that YEAR once per course while Q2 will add it only once, giving different results.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO INSTRUCTOR (ID, NAME, SALARY, DEPT_NAME) VALUES
  (1, 100, 1000, 1),
  (2, 200, 1000, 1),
  (3, 300, 1000, 1),
  (4, 400, 1000, 1),
  (5, 500, 1000, 1);

-- Five instructors teach course 111 in 2020
INSERT INTO TEACHES (ID, COURSE_ID, SEC_ID, YEAR, SEMESTER, INSTRUCTOR) VALUES
  (1, 111, 1, 2020, 1, 1),
  (2, 111, 1, 2020, 1, 2),
  (3, 111, 1, 2020, 1, 3),
  (4, 111, 1, 2020, 1, 4),
  (5, 111, 1, 2020, 1, 5);

-- The same five instructors also teach course 222 in 2020
INSERT INTO TEACHES (ID, COURSE_ID, SEC_ID, YEAR, SEMESTER, INSTRUCTOR) VALUES
  (1, 222, 1, 2020, 1, 1),
  (2, 222, 1, 2020, 1, 2),
  (3, 222, 1, 2020, 1, 3),
  (4, 222, 1, 2020, 1, 4),
  (5, 222, 1, 2020, 1, 5);
counterexample_dsp: Year 2020 has two different courses (111 and 222), each taught by 5 instructors.  Thus every (2020, course) group has COUNT(ID)=5>4.  Q1 sees the year 2020 twice and returns 4040 (2020+2020); Q2 sees it once and returns 2020.

q1: SELECT COURSE_ID, TITLE FROM COURSE
q2: SELECT COURSE_ID, TITLE FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS > 3
explanation: Q1 returns every (COURSE_ID, TITLE) that exists in COURSE, while Q2 adds an additional filter (CREDITS > 3). Any course whose CREDITS value is 3 or less will appear in Q1 but be excluded from Q2, so the two queries are not equivalent.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES
  (1, 100, 10, 4),   -- appears in both Q1 and Q2 (CREDITS > 3)
  (2, 200, 20, 3);   -- appears only in Q1 (CREDITS <= 3)
counterexample_dsp: Insert two courses: one with CREDITS = 4 (passes the Q2 filter) and one with CREDITS = 3 (fails the Q2 filter). Q1 will list both courses; Q2 will list only the one with 4 credits, showing a difference.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT COURSE.COURSE_ID, COURSE.TITLE, TEACHES.ID FROM COURSE JOIN TEACHES WHERE COURSE.COURSE_ID = TEACHES.COURSE_ID AND TEACHES.YEAR = 2010
q2: SELECT DISTINCT COURSE.COURSE_ID, COURSE.TITLE, TEACHES.ID FROM COURSE JOIN TEACHES WHERE COURSE.COURSE_ID >= TEACHES.COURSE_ID AND TEACHES.YEAR = 2010
explanation: Q1 only keeps pairs where COURSE.COURSE_ID equals TEACHES.COURSE_ID, while Q2 keeps pairs where COURSE.COURSE_ID is greater-than-or-equal to TEACHES.COURSE_ID. Therefore, whenever a COURSE row has a larger COURSE_ID than a TEACHES row from year 2010, that pair will appear in Q2 but not in Q1.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO COURSE   (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (10, 100, 1, 3);
INSERT INTO TEACHES (ID, COURSE_ID, SEC_ID, YEAR, SEMESTER, INSTRUCTOR) VALUES (1, 5, 1, 2010, 1, 1);
counterexample_dsp: One COURSE row (COURSE_ID = 10) and one TEACHES row for 2010 (COURSE_ID = 5). Because 10 >= 5 but 10 ≠ 5, the join predicate of Q2 is satisfied while Q1’s equality predicate is not, so Q2 returns one tuple and Q1 returns none.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT INSTRUCTOR.ID, INSTRUCTOR.NAME, TEACHES.COURSE_ID FROM INSTRUCTOR LEFT OUTER JOIN TEACHES ON INSTRUCTOR.ID > TEACHES.ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT INSTRUCTOR.ID, INSTRUCTOR.NAME, TEACHES.COURSE_ID FROM INSTRUCTOR, TEACHES WHERE INSTRUCTOR.ID = TEACHES.ID
explanation:
Q1 keeps **every instructor** (LEFT OUTER JOIN) and tries to match a TEACHES row whose ID is *smaller* (INSTRUCTOR.ID > TEACHES.ID).  If no such lower-ID row exists, TEACHES.COURSE_ID is returned as NULL.  
Q2 is a plain inner join that only returns rows where the two IDs are **equal**.  Therefore an instructor for which the only TEACHES rows have the *same* ID (no smaller one) will produce a NULL course in Q1 but a real course id in Q2, so the result sets differ.
counterexample_dsp:
One instructor (ID = 10) and one teaches row (also ID = 10).
• In Q1 the join condition 10 > 10 is false, so the instructor survives with COURSE_ID = NULL.
• In Q2 the equality join matches and returns COURSE_ID = 100.

q1: WITH S AS (SELECT ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR FROM TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID)>4) SELECT DISTINCT ID,NAME FROM S NATURAL JOIN STUDENT
q2: WITH S AS (SELECT ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR FROM TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID)>5) SELECT DISTINCT ID,NAME FROM S NATURAL JOIN STUDENT
explanation:
No counter-example can be built because the two queries are logically equivalent.
After the natural join each row is grouped by the triple (ID , TIME_SLOT_ID , YEAR).
Inside such a group the value of TIME_SLOT_ID is, by definition, constant, therefore
  COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID)
can only evaluate to 0 (if TIME_SLOT_ID is NULL) or to 1 (if it is not NULL).
Hence the HAVING conditions “> 4” (Q1) and “> 5” (Q2) are both impossible to satisfy; the CTE S is always empty, and the final SELECT returns no rows for both queries. Because there is no legal data that makes COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID) equal to 5 (or anything larger than 1) in this grouping, the result sets of Q1 and Q2 are identical for every possible database state.
counterexample_dsp: Not applicable – the queries are equivalent, therefore no database state can make them diverge.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS=(SELECT MAX(CREDITS) FROM COURSE)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE AS C JOIN (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) AS MAX_CREDITS FROM COURSE GROUP BY DEPT_NAME) AS A WHERE C.CREDITS = A.MAX_CREDITS
explanation: Q1 looks for departments that own **the overall highest-credit course in the whole table**.  Q2 first computes each department’s local MAX(credits), but then (because the join has **no condition that ties the sub-query rows back to the same department**) it matches every course whose credits equal *any* department’s local maximum.  Therefore a department whose own maximum is *not* the global maximum can still be returned by Q2 if some of its courses share the same credit value as another department’s maximum.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES
  (1, 101, 1, 4),   -- Dept 1, global-max credits
  (2, 102, 1, 3),   -- another course in Dept 1
  (3, 201, 2, 4),   -- Dept 2, also global-max credits
  (4, 301, 3, 2);   -- Dept 3, max only 2 (should not be in Q1 but appears in Q2)
counterexample_dsp: Dept 1 and Dept 2 both have 4-credit courses; those 4 credits are the global maximum.  Dept 3’s own maximum is only 2, so it should not appear in Q1.  But because 2 is also a local maximum (of Dept 3 itself) the un-qualified join in Q2 makes the 2-credit course of Dept 3 match that 2, so Dept 3 is erroneously returned by Q2.
